## Introduction
This project requires some background in Calculus and analysis in several variables
In particular you should know about the partial derivatives of a function in several variables, as well as the chain rule in several variables. 

In machine learning one tries to find a function which approximates a given set of measurement data in a best possible way.
For this to be possible computationally, we require that the candidate functions have a given form. 
If the measurement data is $\mathbf{x}_i\in\mathbb{R}^n$, $\mathbf{y}_i\in\mathbb{R}^n$, 
we would like to find an  $\mathbf{F}$ on the given form so that ''the total error''
$$\sum_{i=1}^m | \mathbf{F}(\mathbf{x}_i)-\mathbf{y}_i |^2$$
in the measurement data is as small as possible. We assume that the functions on the given form are uniquely described by a set of *parameters* $w_1,w_2,...$, 
and we then write 
$$\mathbf{F}_{w_1,w_2,...}: \mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^n$$
for $\mathbf{F}$. 
Our question becomes: Which choice of parameters gives a function $\mathbf{F}_{w_1,w_2,...}$ with total error 
$$f(w_1,w_2,...)=\sum_{i=1}^m | \mathbf{F}_{w_1,w_2,...}(\mathbf{x}_i)-\mathbf{y}_i |^2.$$ {#eq-find-min}
as small as possible? This is a minimisation problem where $w_1,w_2,...$ are the variables (not $\mathbf{x}_i$ and $\mathbf{y}_i$, these are given measurement data!). 
The total error @eq-find-min is also called the *loss function*.

To find the $w_1,w_2,...$ which gives the minimum of @eq-find-min turns out to be difficult.
To find good approximations to this minimum can be simpler: 
From analysis in several variables we know that the *gradient* of a function $f:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}$,
$$\nabla f = \begin{pmatrix} \frac{\partial f}{\partial x_1}, \frac{\partial f}{\partial x_2},...,\frac{\partial f}{\partial x_n}\end{pmatrix},$$
points in the direction where $f$ increases the most. Therefore, the function will decrease the most if we move in the direction of the negative gradient, 
and this is exactly what we will do:
We compute the gradient of $f$ given by @eq-find-min, and follow this a little, to reach a point where $f$ has a smaller value. 

We will require our candidate function to be on the following form. 
$$
\mathbf{F}_{\mathbf{w}^{(1)},\mathbf{b}^{(1)},\mathbf{w}^{(2)},\mathbf{b}^{(2)},...} = \mathbf{F}_1(\mathbf{F}_2(\cdots \mathbf{F}_r(\mathbf{x})))
$$ {#eq-neuralnet}
where all $\mathbf{w}^{(k)}$, $\mathbf{b}^{(k)}$ are vectors of length $n$, and where
$$
\mathbf{F}_k(\mathbf{x}) = \sigma(W^{(k)}\mathbf{x}+\mathbf{b}^{(k)}),
$$
with
$$
W^{(k)}=
\begin{pmatrix}
w_1^{(k)} & w_n^{(k)} & w_{n-1}^{(k)} & \cdots & w_2^{(k)} \\ 
w_2^{(k)} & w_1^{(k)} & w_n^{(k)} & \cdots & w_3^{(k)} \\
w_3^{(k)} & w_2^{(k)} & w_1^{(k)} & \cdots & w_4^{(k)} \\
\vdots & \vdots & \vdots & \vdots & \vdots \\
w_n^{(k)} & w_{n-1}^{(k)} & w_{n-2}^{(k)} & \cdots & w_1^{(k)}
\end{pmatrix}.
$$
Some comments are in order:

* $W^{(k)}$ is a special type of matrix which is constant along diagonals. 
Such matrices are called *circulant Toeplitz matrices*, and have a series of nice properties which can be useful in machine learning. 
There also exist effective algorithms to multiply with such matrices, something which is exploited in the function \texttt{cconv}, to be defined later. 
\texttt{cconv} takes two vectors $\mathbf{w}$ and $\mathbf{x}$ as input, and returns $W\mathbf{x}$, where $W$ is the circulant Toeplitz matrix with first column being $\mathbf{w}$. 
* $\sigma:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^n$ over is the (component-wise) *activation function*.
This is first defined from $\mathbb{R}$ to $\mathbb{R}$ by $\sigma(x)=1/(1+e^{-x})$, and extended component-wise to $\mathbb{R}^n$ by
$$
\sigma(\mathbf{x})=\sigma\begin{pmatrix} x_1 \\ x_2 \\ \vdots \\ x_n \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} \sigma(x_1) \\ \sigma(x_2) \\ \vdots \\ \sigma(x_n) \end{pmatrix}.
$$
* @eq-neuralnet is also called a *Neural Net* (NN), and the $\mathbf{F}_k$'s are called its *layers*. 
We see that the parameters of the candidate functions are split in groups, as dictated by the vectors $\mathbf{w}^{(i)}$, $\mathbf{b}^{(i)}$. 
When the $W^{(i)}$ are circulant Toeplitz matrices (as we require), the neural net is called a *Convolutional Neural Net* (CNN). 
In a general neural net the $W^{(i)}$ can have other forms as well, 
and it can be the case that some of the $W^{(i)}$ are circulant Toeplitz matrices, while others are not. 

Since @eq-neuralnet is a composition of many functions, we must use the *chain rule* in several variables to find the gradient of @eq-find-min. 
For this we need to find the *Jacobians* of the ''inner functions" in @eq-neuralnet. 
The Jacobian of $\mathbf{F}(\mathbf{x}):\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^m$, denoted $\mathbf{F}'(\mathbf{x})$, is defined as the $m\times n$-matrix
$$
\begin{pmatrix} 
\frac{\partial F_1}{\partial x_1} & \frac{\partial F_1}{\partial x_2} & \cdots & \frac{\partial F_1}{\partial x_n} \\
\frac{\partial F_2}{\partial x_1} & \frac{\partial F_2}{\partial x_2} & \cdots & \frac{\partial F_2}{\partial x_n} \\
\vdots                                       & \vdots                                       & \vdots & \vdots \\
\frac{\partial F_m}{\partial x_1} & \frac{\partial F_m}{\partial x_2} & \cdots & \frac{\partial F_m}{\partial x_n} \\                 
\end{pmatrix}
$$
where $F_1,F_2,...,F_m$ are the component functions of $\mathbf{F}$. The chain rule can now be formulated as follows..

::: {#thm-teorem1}
Let $\mathbf{F}: \mathbb{R}^k\to\mathbb{R}^m$, $\mathbf{G}: \mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^k$ be functions with continuous partial derivatives. 
Then the composite function $\mathbf{H}(\mathbf{x})=\mathbf{F}(\mathbf{G}(\mathbf{x}))$ also has continuous partial derivatives, and
$$\mathbf{H}'(\mathbf{x})=\mathbf{F}'(\mathbf{G}(\mathbf{x}))\mathbf{G}'(\mathbf{x}).$$
:::

We thus obtain the Jacobian of a composite function by multiplying the Jacobians of the involved functions
\footnote{The requirement of continuous partial derivative is actually stricter than what we need}.
In particular we need the Jacobian of the activation function, so let us start with this. 

::: {#exr-1ml}
Show that $\sigma'(x)=\sigma(x)(1-\sigma(x))$

::::: {.content-visible when-profile="instructor"}
::::::: {.callout-important title='Solution' collapse="true"}
We have
$$\sigma'(x)=\frac{e^{-x}}{(1+e^{-x})^2}=\frac{1}{1+e^{-x}}\frac{e^{-x}}{1+e^{-x}}=\sigma(x)\left(1-\frac{1}{1+e^{-x}}\right)=\sigma(x)(1-\sigma(x)).$$
:::::::
:::::
:::

The component-wise extension of the activation function thus has the diagonal matrix with  $\sigma'(x_i)$ on the diagonal as Jacobian.

Given measurement data $\mathbf{x}_i\in\mathbb{R}^n$, $\mathbf{y}_i\in\mathbb{R}^n$, we would like to find vectors $\mathbf{w}^{(i)}$, $\mathbf{b}^{(i)}$ 
that gives a neural net @eq-neuralnet with minimum total error
$$
f\left( \mathbf{w}^{(1)},\mathbf{b}^{(1)},\mathbf{w}^{(2)},\mathbf{b}^{(2)},... \right)
= \sum_{i=1}^m | \mathbf{F}_{\mathbf{w}^{(1)},\mathbf{b}^{(1)},\mathbf{w}^{(2)},\mathbf{b}^{(2)},...}(\mathbf{x}_i)-\mathbf{y}_i |^2.
$$
When we compute the gradient of this we will write $\mathbf{F}_1\circ\mathbf{F}_2$ for the composite function $\mathbf{x}\to \mathbf{F}_1(\mathbf{F}_2(\mathbf{x}))$, 
and more generally $\mathbf{F}_1\circ\cdots\circ\mathbf{F}_r$ for the composite function $\mathbf{x}\to\mathbf{F}_1(\mathbf{F}_2(\cdots \mathbf{F}_r(\mathbf{x})))$. 

Let us now look at the individual layers. To apply the chain rule correctly we need to set up the points where we evaluate the Jacobians. For this we define

$$\begin{aligned}
\mathbf{z}^{(2r)}     &=\mathbf{x}    &\\
\mathbf{z}^{(2k-1)} &=W^{(k)}\mathbf{z}^{(2k)}+\mathbf{b}^{(k)} &1\leq k\leq r \\
\mathbf{z}^{(2k-2)} &=\sigma(\mathbf{z}^{(2k-1)}) & 1\leq k\leq r.
\end{aligned}$$ {#eq-yzdef}

The first layer can be written
$$
\mathbf{F}_r: 
\begin{pmatrix} 
\mathbf{w}^{(1)} \\
\mathbf{b}^{(1)}  \\
\vdots \\
\mathbf{w}^{(r-1)} \\
\mathbf{b}^{(r-1)} \\
\mathbf{w}^{(r)} \\
\mathbf{b}^{(r)}
\end{pmatrix} 
\to
\begin{pmatrix} 
\mathbf{w}^{(1)} \\
\mathbf{b}^{(1)}  \\
\vdots \\
\mathbf{w}^{(r-1)} \\
\mathbf{b}^{(r-1)} \\
\sigma\left(W^{(r)}\mathbf{x} +\mathbf{b}^{(r)}\right)
\end{pmatrix},
$$
We have here re-defined $\mathbf{F}_r$ in the sense that the variables, with the exception of $\mathbf{w}^{(r)},\mathbf{b}^{(r)}$, are forwarded to the next layer. 
We continue like this, so that we eliminate the $\mathbf{w}$ and $\mathbf{b}$-variables, layer by layer. 
Let us find the Jacobian $\mathbf{F}_r'$, and let us start with the last $n$ component functions, which have the form 
$$ \left( \mathbf{w}^{(1)},\mathbf{b}^{(1)},...,\mathbf{w}^{(r)},\mathbf{b}^{(r)}\right) \to \sigma(\mathbf{G}(\mathbf{w}^{(r)},\mathbf{b}^{(r)}))$$
with $\mathbf{G}(\mathbf{w}^{(r)},\mathbf{b}^{(r)}) = W^{(r)}\mathbf{x} +\mathbf{b}^{(r)}$. 



::: {#exr-2ml}
Let $\mathbf{G}(\mathbf{x})=W\mathbf{x} + \mathbf{b}$, where $W$ be an $n\times n$ matrix, and $\mathbf{b},\mathbf{x}\in\mathbb{R}^n$ . Show that $\mathbf{G}'(\mathbf{x})=W$. 

:::

::: {#exr-3ml}
Let instead $\mathbf{G}: \mathbb{R}^{2n}\to\mathbb{R}^n$ be defined by
$$
\mathbf{G}\left( w_1,...,w_n,b_1,...,b_n\right) =
\begin{pmatrix}
w_1 & w_n & w_{n-1} & \cdots & w_2 \\ 
w_2 & w_1 & w_n & \cdots & w_3 \\
w_3 & w_2 & w_1 & \cdots & w_4 \\
\vdots & \vdots & \vdots & \vdots & \vdots \\
w_n & w_{n-1} & w_{n-2} & \cdots & w_1
\end{pmatrix}
\mathbf{x}+\mathbf{b}.
$$
In other words, we now consider $w_i$ and $b_i$ as variables, and $\mathbf{x}$ as a constant. 
Show that
$$
\mathbf{G}'(w_1,...,w_n,b_1,...,b_n) = 
\left(
\begin{array}{ccccc|ccccc}
x_1 & x_n & x_{n-1} & \cdots & x_2 & 1 & 0 & 0 & \cdots & 0 \\
x_2 & x_1 & x_n & \cdots & x_3 & 0 & 1 & 0 & \cdots & 0 \\
x_3 & x_2 & x_1 & \cdots & x_4 & 0 & 0 & 1 & \cdots & 0 \\
\vdots & \vdots & \vdots & \vdots & \vdots & \vdots & \vdots & \vdots & \vdots & \vdots\\
x_n & x_{n-1} & x_{n-2} & \cdots & x_1 & 0 & 0 & 0 & \cdots & 1 \\
\end{array}
\right)
$$ {#eq-jacobinew}

::::: {.content-visible when-profile="instructor"}
::::::: {.callout-important title='Solution' collapse="true"}
Component function $i$ of $\mathbf{G}$ can be written
$$
G_i\left( w_1,...,w_n,b_1,...,b_n \right)  = \sum_{j=1}^{n} w_{i-j+1}x_j + b_i = \sum_{j=1}^{n} w_jx_{i-j+1} + b_i ,
$$
so that $\frac{\partial G_i }{\partial w_j}=x_{i-j+1}$. This proves the expression for the left part of the matrix @eq-jacobinew. 
We also have that
$$\frac{\partial G_i}{\partial b_j}=\begin{cases} 0 & \text{ for } j\neq i \\ 1 & \text{ for } j=i\end{cases},$$
which explains why the right part of the matrix @eq-jacobinew is the identity matrix.
:::::::
:::::
:::

Since $\sigma\left(W^{(r)}\mathbf{x} +\mathbf{b}^{(r)}\right)$ does not depend on $\mathbf{w}^{(1)}$, $\mathbf{b}^{(1)}$,..., $\mathbf{w}^{(r-1)}$, $\mathbf{b}^{(r-1)}$, 
the last $n$ component functions in $\mathbf{F}_r$ will therefore have Jacobian $\left(\begin{array}{c|c}O & U^{(r)}\end{array}\right)$, where

$$
U^{(r)} :=
\sigma'(\mathbf{z}^{(2r-1)})
\left(\begin{array}{cccc|cccc}
x_1 & x_n   & \cdots  & x_2               & 1 & 0 & \cdots & 0 \\
x_2 & x_1   & \cdots   & x_3                & 0 & 1 & \cdots & 0 \\
\vdots     & \vdots       & \vdots  & \vdots               & \vdots & \vdots & \vdots & \vdots \\
x_n     & x_{n-1}        & \cdots & x_1            & 0 & 0 & \cdots & 1 
\end{array}\right),
$$ {#eq-urdef}


which is an $n\times n$ diagonal matrix multiplied with a $n\times(2n)$ matrix. 
Since the first component functions are simply the identity mapping, we also get
$$
\mathbf{F}_r'=
\left(\begin{array}{c|c}
I          & O \\ \hline
O & U^{(r)}
\end{array}\right),
$$ {#eq-firstexpr}
In the same way we write the other layers $\mathbf{F}_1$,...,$\mathbf{F}_{r-1}$ as
$$
\mathbf{F}_k: 
\begin{pmatrix} 
\mathbf{w}^{(1)} \\
\mathbf{b}^{(1)} \\
\vdots \\
\mathbf{w}^{(k-1)} \\
\mathbf{b}^{(k-1)}\\
\mathbf{w}^{(k)} \\
\mathbf{b}^{(k)} \\
\mathbf{x}
\end{pmatrix} 
\to
\begin{pmatrix} 
\mathbf{w}^{(1)} \\
\mathbf{b}^{(1)} \\
\vdots \\
\mathbf{w}^{(k-1)} \\
\mathbf{b}^{(k-1)}\\
\sigma\left(W^{(k)}\mathbf{x} +\mathbf{b}^{(k)}\right)
\end{pmatrix},$$
where $1\leq k\leq r-1$. The only difference from the above is that there are $n$ extra variables $x_i$ here (we shall evaluate in $\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{z}^{(2k-1)}$). 
This means that the only difference for $\mathbf{F}'_k$, when comparing with $\mathbf{F}'_r$ in @eq-firstexpr, is that we get extra columns 
$\begin{pmatrix} O \\ V^{(k)} \end{pmatrix}$ on the end, where 
$$
V^{(k)} := 
\sigma'(\mathbf{z}^{(2k-1)})
\left(\begin{array}{cccc}
w_1^{(k)} & w_n^{(k)}   & \cdots  & w_2^{(k)}           \\
w_2^{(k)} & w_1^{(k)}   & \cdots   & w_3^{(k)}           \\
\vdots     & \vdots       & \vdots  & \vdots               \\
w_n^{(k)}     & w_{n-1}^{(k)}        & \cdots & w_1^{(k)}         
\end{array}\right)
$$ {#eq-computevk}
(this is the Jacobian of $\mathbf{x}\to \sigma\left(W^{(k)}\mathbf{x} + \mathbf{b}\right)$). 
The other columns are deduced in the same way as @eq-urdef, giving
$\left(\begin{array}{c|c} I & O \\ \hline O & U^{(k)}\end{array}\right)$, where
$$
U^{(k)} :=
\sigma'(\mathbf{z}^{(2k-1)})
\left(\begin{array}{cccc|cccc}
z_1^{(2k)} & z_n^{(2k)}   & \cdots  & z_2^{(2k)}               & 1 & 0 & \cdots & 0 \\
z_2^{(2k)} & z_1^{(2k)}   & \cdots   & z_3^{(2k)}                & 0 & 1 & \cdots & 0 \\
\vdots     & \vdots       & \vdots  & \vdots               & \vdots & \vdots & \vdots & \vdots \\
z_n^{(2k)}     & z_{n-1}^{(2k)}        & \cdots & z_1^{(2k)}            & 0 & 0 & \cdots & 1 
\end{array}\right)
$$ {#eq-computeuk}
($\mathbf{x}$ in @eq-urdef is exchanged with $\mathbf{z}^{(2k)}$). In other words we get
$$
\mathbf{F}_k'=
\left(\begin{array}{c|c|c}
I         & O & O \\ \hline
O & U^{(k)} & V^{(k)}
\end{array}\right).
$$

Now that we have the Jacobian of each individual layer, we can use the chain rule to find the Jacobian of the entire neural net. 
If we first apply the chain rule to find the Jacobian of $\mathbf{F}_{r-1}\circ\mathbf{F}_r$ we get
$$
\left(\begin{array}{c|c|c}
I_1     & O       &O           \\ \hline
O & U^{(r-1)}  & V^{(r-1)} 
\end{array} \right) 
\left(\begin{array}{c|c|c} 
I_1     & O & O \\ \hline 
O & I_2     & O \\ \hline 
O  & O & U^{(r)}
\end{array}\right).
$$ {#eq-oppg1}
Here we split the identity matrix $I$ into $\left(\begin{array}{c|c} I_1 & O \\ \hline O & I_2 \end{array}\right)$, 
for the rows to match the columns in the preceding matrix. 

::: {#exr-4ml}
Show that qeq-oppg1 equals
$$
\left(\begin{array}{c|c|c} 
I_1     & O & O \\ \hline
O & U^{(r-1)} & V^{(r-1)}U^{(r)}
\end{array}\right)
$$

:::

The Jacobian of  $\mathbf{F}_{r-2}\circ\mathbf{F}_{r-1}\circ\mathbf{F}_r$ now becomes
$$
\left(\begin{array}{c|c|c}
I_1     & O  & O             \\ \hline
O & U^{(r-2)}  & V^{(r-2)} 
\end{array} \right)
\left(\begin{array}{c|c|c|c} 
I_1     & O & O & O \\ \hline
O & I_2     & O & O \\ \hline 
O & O & U^{(r-1)} & V^{(r-1)}U^{(r)}
\end{array}\right),
$$ {#eq-oppg2}

::: {#exr-5ml}
Show that @eq-oppg2 becomes
$$
\left(\begin{array}{c|c|c|c} 
I_1     & O & O & O \\ \hline
O & U^{(r-2)} & V^{(r-2)} U^{(r-1)} & V^{(r-2)} V^{(r-1)}U^{(r)}
\end{array}\right)
$$

:::

If we continue this process to include all layers, we get that the $k$'th part in the end becomes. 
$$
V^{(1)}\cdots V^{(k-1)}U^{(k)}.
$$ {#eq-kthpart}
What remains now is to also apply the Jacobian (=gradient) of the outer function.

::: {#exr-6ml}
Let $g(\mathbf{x})=\sum_{i=1}^m |\mathbf{F}(\mathbf{x}_i)-\mathbf{y_i}|^2$, where $\mathbf{F}$ is a differentiable functions. Show that 
$$\nabla g = \sum_{i=1}^m 2(\mathbf{F}(\mathbf{x}_i)-\mathbf{y}_i)^T\mathbf{F}'(\mathbf{x}_i).$$

:::

If we combine @eq-kthpart with @exr-6ml, the $k$'th part of the gradient for the whole neural net becomes (in the case of one measurement point)
$$
2(\mathbf{z}_0-\mathbf{y})^TV^{(1)}\cdots V^{(k-1)}U^{(k)}.
$$ {#eq-kthpartgrad}
The first half of this matrix are the partial derivatives for the $w_i^{(k)}$-variables, the second half those of the $b_i^{(k)}$ variables.

## Implementation
Let us take a look at how all this can be implemented. The algorithm for following the gradient to get closer to a minimum of the loss function is called 
*backpropagation*. The entire implementation can be found in the file \texttt{testml.py}. 
The algorithm takes the measurements $\mathbf{x}_i$ and $\mathbf{y}_i$, the number of layers $r$, 
and the number of iterations \texttt{its}, as input, 
and returns the updated parameters $\mathbf{w}^{(i)}$ and $\mathbf{b}^{(i)}$, after this number of iterations. 
As before we assume that all matrices are $n\times n$, 
all vectors have length $n$, and that there are $m$ measurement points, which we will randomly generate.

We need functions that implement the activation function, as well as multiplication with its Jacobian, and a function that implements circular convolution:

```{pyodide-python}
#| autorun: true
def sigma(x):
    return 1/(1+np.exp(-x))

def sigmader(x):
    return sigma(x)*(1-sigma(x))

def cconv(x, y):
    X = np.fft.fft(x)
    Y = np.fft.fft(y)
    Z = X*Y
    return np.fft.ifft(Z).real
```

We also need code that computes the current value of the lossfunction:
```{pyodide-python}
#| autorun: true
def loss(x, y, w, b):
    n, m = np.shape(x)
    n, r = np.shape(w)
    loss = 0
    for t in range(m):          # Iterate through the measurements
        z = np.zeros(n)
        for k in range(r,0,-1): # iterate through the layers
            z = cconv(w[:,k-1], z) + b[:,k-1]
            z = sigma(z)
        loss += sum(abs(z-y[:,t])**2)
    return loss
```


We now have all we need to implement the backpropagation function:
```{pyodide-python}
#| autorun: true
def backpropagation(x, y, r, its):
    valp = 0
    lrate = 0.01  # Learning rate
    n, m = np.shape(x)
    w = np.random.rand(n, r) # Randomly generated initial parameters
    b = np.random.rand(n, r) # Randomly generated initial parameters
    for it in range(its):
        dw = np.zeros_like(w)
        db = np.zeros_like(b)
        for t in range(m):
            z = np.zeros((n,2*r+1))
            z[:,2*r] = x[:,t]
            for k in range(r,0,-1):
                z[:, 2*k-1] = cconv(w[:,k-1], z[:,2*k]) + b[:,k-1]
                z[:, 2*k-2] = sigma(z[:,2*k-1])
            
            temp = 2*(z[:,0]-y[:,t])
            for k in range(1,r+1):
                temp = temp*sigmader(z[:,2*k-1])
                dw[:,k-1] += cconv( np.flip(z[:,2*k]), temp)
                db[:,k-1] += temp
                temp = cconv( np.flip(w[:,k-1]), temp)
        w = w - lrate*dw
        b = b - lrate*db
        print(loss(x, y, w, b))
    return w, b
```
This code requires several comments. 
The implementation has randomly generated initial values for the weights $\mathbf{w}^{(k)}$ and $\mathbf{b}^{(k)}$. 
These are stored in $n\times r$-matrices, where each column represents a layer. 
The outer \texttt{for}-loop in the code goes through the iterations. 
Each iteration follows the gradient a small bit from the current point to reach a new point. 
In the next iteration the gradient at the new point is computed, and this is followed a little bit from the new point, and so on. 
The update of the point by following the gradient a small bit is captured by the two last lines in the outermost \texttt{for}-loop. 
There the *hyperparameter* \texttt{lrate} is seen, which captures the distance to follow the gradient. 
In machine learning this is also called the *learning rate*, and the algorithm is highly sensitive to this parameter:
Following the gradient for a little while corresponds to using a first order approximation to the function. 
But this approximation is good only near the point we evaluate in. We should therefore not follow the gradient too far. We should not follow it too short either - 
that would render the algorithm ineffective. In practice a compromise is struck. An algorithm can also set the learning rate adaptively, 
as some points may allow for following the gradient longer than others.

The next \texttt{for}-loop goes through the $m$ data points. For each of them 
the vectors $\mathbf{z}^{(k)}$ in @eq-yzdef are computed. This is called the *forward pass* of the algorithm,
and is done by applying the activation function and multiplication with $W^{(k)}$ in alternating order (line 14-15). 
Once this has been done, the expression @eq-kthpartgrad for the different parts of the gradient is computed. 
This is also called the *backward pass* of the algorithm since, as we will see, the order of the computations will be reversed when compared to the forward pass. 
Let us look at why this is the case.

::: {#exr-7ml}
Assume we would like to compute the expression $\mathbf{x}^TA_1A_2\cdots A_n$ on a computer, 
where $\mathbf{x}\in\mathbb{R}^n$ and the $A_i$ are $n\times n$-matrices.  
Explain, in terms of arithmetic complexity, why one should attempt to compute this expression from left to right, rather than from right to left.

::::: {.content-visible when-profile="instructor"}
::::::: {.callout-important title='Solution' collapse="true"}
When this is done from left to right you compute a series of vector-matrix multiplications. 
For the opposite way one computes a series of matrix-matrix multiplications (except for the last one). 
The point is simply that vector-matrix multiplications are easier to compute than matrix-matrix multiplications.
:::::::
:::::
:::

In terms of complexity it is preferable to compute the quantities from left to right, i.e., in order opposite to the forward pass. 
When computing @eq-kthpartgrad from left to right, $2(\mathbf{z}_0-\mathbf{y})^TV^{(1)}\cdots V^{(k)}$ can be obtained from 
$2(\mathbf{z}_0-\mathbf{y})^TV^{(1)}\cdots V^{(k-1)}$ by multiplying with $V^{(k)}$ to the right. 
Our implementation exploits this by storing the $2(\mathbf{z}_0-\mathbf{y})^TV^{(1)}\cdots V^{(k)}$ in the temporary variable \texttt{temp}.
According to @eq-computevk, this can be done by

* first multiplying with $\sigma'(\mathbf{z}^{(2k-1)})$ to the right (first line in the innermost \texttt{for}-loop), 
* then multiplying with $W^{(k)}$ to the right (circular convolution with the reverse of $\mathbf{w}^{(k)}$. Last line in the innermost \texttt{for}-loop). 

To get the partial derivatives w.r.t. the $\mathbf{w}^{(k)}$ and the $\mathbf{b}^{(k)}$ (the $k$'th part of the gradient), 
we multiply with $U^{(k)}$ to the right. According to @eq-computeuk this can be done by
first multiplying with $\sigma'(\mathbf{z}^{(2k-1)})$ to the right (first line in the innermost \texttt{for}-loop). After this,

* storing this gives partial derivatives w.r.t. the $\mathbf{b}^{(k)}$ (third line in the innermost \texttt{for}-loop),
* circular convolution with the reverse of $\mathbf{z}^{(2k)}$ gives partial derivatives w.r.t. the $\mathbf{w}^{(k)}$ (second line in the innermost \texttt{for}-loop), 

After the innermost \texttt{for}-loop the gradient at the current point (captured by the variables \texttt{dw} and \texttt{db}) 
has been updated with the contribution from one more data point.



Code for invoking backpropagation can now be as follows.
```{pyodide-python}
#| autorun: true
m = 10   # Number of data points
n = 10   # dimension of the data
its = 10 # Number of iterations
r = 10   # Number of layers

x = np.random.rand(n,m) # Randomly generated measurements
y = np.random.rand(n,m) # Randomly generated measurements

w, b = backpropagation(x, y, r, its)
```



::: {#exr-8ml}
If you run the code you will see that the loss function usually decreases in the iterations. Is this always the case? 
If you increase the learning rate to 0.1, will the loss function decrease when you run the code? 
If the loss function increases in some iterations, can you think of a way to adjust the learning rate so that the loss function always decreases?

:::
